papers.note: The reference mixture of experts design that made sparse trillion parameter models practical.
papers.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
papers.explain_beginner: The question here is whether a language model can be made dramatically bigger, meaning it holds far more learned parameters, without making it proportionally slower or more expensive to run. Standard transformer models use every single parameter for every word they process, so doubling the model size roughly doubles the computation needed. Fedus, Zoph and Shazeer instead built a model that activates only a small piece of itself for each word, called a sparse mixture of experts, so the total parameter count can grow into the trillions while the actual computation per word stays close to that of a much smaller dense model. They found this approach trained noticeably faster than the standard dense recipe for a given compute budget, and worked consistently across text in 101 different languages. What the paper does not settle is whether such enormous sparse models are worth the engineering cost, they still need enough memory across many machines to hold all the experts even though they only use a few per word, and training a first trillion parameter model of this kind exposed instability problems that took real engineering effort to fix.
papers.explain_business: For an organization deciding how to spend a fixed training compute budget, this paper's practical claim is that sparse expert routing can turn the same GPU or TPU hours into a model that reaches a given quality level up to 4 to 7 times faster than a standard dense model of comparable pretraining setup, or into a substantially more capable model for the same wall clock time. That is a real lever for teams training their own foundation models rather than only fine tuning existing ones. The condition to know before betting on this approach is that the savings are in compute time, not hardware footprint, a trillion parameter sparse model still needs enough combined memory across a cluster to hold every expert, so it suits organizations that already run multi accelerator training clusters more than those hoping to shrink a single server's footprint. It is also now the reference design that later mixture of experts production models built on and refined, so its tradeoffs are a reasonable baseline for evaluating any vendor claiming mixture of experts efficiency.
papers.explain_practitioner: Switch Transformer replaces the standard Mixture-of-Experts routing, which sends each token to multiple experts, with a simplified top-1 router that sends each token to exactly one expert, cutting communication and routing overhead. Built on the T5 pretraining recipe and evaluated against T5-Base, T5-Large and T5-XXL baselines, the switch routed models delivered up to a 7x pretraining speedup over T5-Base and T5-Large under matched compute, and a 4x speedup over T5-XXL, while scaling a sparsely activated model to a trillion parameters on the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus. On multilingual mT5-Base comparisons the approach improved results across all 101 languages tested, not just a subset. A key engineering contribution the authors report is stabilizing training enough to use lower precision bfloat16 arithmetic for large sparse models, something earlier Mixture-of-Experts work could not do reliably. The tradeoff the authors acknowledge is that these gains come from wall clock and sample efficiency during pretraining, not from a smaller footprint, the trillion parameter model still requires distributed memory across many accelerators to store its experts.

papers.note: Peer reviewed architecture taxonomy covering training pipelines, datasets and deployment issues in one place.
papers.title: A Review on Large Language Models: Architectures, Applications, Taxonomies, Open Issues and Challenges
papers.authors: Mohaimenul Azam Khan Raiaan et al.
papers.explain_beginner: This paper does not run a new experiment, instead it asks a mapping question, given how fast large language models have multiplied since ChatGPT's release, can one document pull together how they are built, trained, used, and where they still fall short, in a way a newcomer or a busy practitioner can actually use? Raiaan and coauthors trace the history of these text generating AI systems from earlier language models up through the transformer based systems in wide use today, explain the standard pipeline of pretraining then fine tuning then alignment with human feedback, and catalog real applications across fields including healthcare, education, agriculture, and business. The review found that despite the pace of progress, unresolved problems, like factual errors the model states confidently, high computational cost, and difficulty adapting safely to sensitive domains, show up repeatedly across nearly every application area they surveyed. As a review rather than new research, it does not itself resolve any of these open problems, it organizes and names them so future work has a clearer target.
papers.explain_business: For a team trying to get oriented before making an AI investment decision, this kind of review is useful as a single reference point that lays out what current large language models can plausibly do well, translation, summarization, question answering, code assistance, against the practical constraints, inference cost, hallucination risk, and domain adaptation difficulty, that determine whether a specific use case is ready to deploy now or needs more groundwork first. It is explicitly not a source of new performance numbers or a comparison of specific vendor models, so it should not be used to pick between competing products. Its business value is in scoping conversations, helping a team new to this technology understand which problems, like factual reliability or high serving cost, are known, active, unsolved research areas rather than something a vendor's product update will quietly fix, and which application domains, per the survey's own examples in healthcare and education, already have documented deployment patterns worth learning from before committing budget.
papers.explain_practitioner: This is a structured survey rather than an empirical study, it synthesizes the large language model literature along five threads, historical evolution from earlier neural language models to current transformer architectures, the mechanics of the transformer itself, the standard three stage training pipeline of pretraining, supervised fine tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback, the datasets and compute resources that pipeline depends on, and deployment patterns across domains including biomedical and healthcare, education, agriculture, and general business use. Because it is a review, there is no single benchmark result or baseline comparison to report, its contribution is the taxonomy itself and the systematic cataloging of open issues, which the authors group by technical causes, hallucination, high inference and training cost, limited context handling, and by practical deployment barriers, data privacy, domain adaptation, and evaluation gaps. The authors' own framing acknowledges the review's core limitation, a field moving this fast means any single snapshot taxonomy risks being outdated by the time newer architectures or training techniques become standard practice.

papers.note: Trains a diffusion model rather than an autoregressive one at 8B scale and reaches comparable results, challenging the assumption that core language-model capability depends on next-token prediction.
papers.title: Large Language Diffusion Models
papers.explain_beginner: Almost every well known AI language model, including ChatGPT, generates text by predicting one word at a time, left to right. This paper asked whether that particular method is actually necessary for a model to become fluent and capable, or whether a very different training approach could work just as well. The researchers built LLaDA, an 8 billion parameter model trained with a diffusion method borrowed from image generating AI, where the model learns by having words randomly hidden and then practicing filling them back in, eventually learning to generate whole passages by repeatedly cleaning up a mostly blanked out draft. Tested on reasoning, math, and coding tasks, it performed close to, and on some tasks better than, a similarly sized model built the standard way. It also handled a known weakness of standard models, called the reversal curse, noticeably better. This does not mean diffusion will replace the standard approach, only that the standard approach is a choice, not the only path to a capable language model.
papers.explain_business: For organizations making long term bets on model architecture, this paper is evidence, not yet a product recommendation, that the autoregressive next word prediction approach underlying almost every commercial LLM today is not the only viable path to a competent language model. That matters strategically because it widens the field of plausible future architectures rather than confirming any current alternative is ready to deploy. As the authors note, LLaDA still lacks the inference speed optimizations, RLHF based alignment for safety and instruction following, and multimodal support that production systems require, so it is not something a business should adopt directly today. The realistic near term relevance is for teams tracking the research frontier on inference cost and architecture diversity, since a maturing diffusion based alternative could eventually offer different speed or robustness trade offs, but that is a multi year horizon, not an immediate deployment consideration.
papers.explain_practitioner: LLaDA is an 8 billion parameter language model trained from scratch using a diffusion objective rather than next token prediction. Training randomly masks tokens at rate t and trains a Transformer to predict the masked tokens by optimizing a variational lower bound, while generation starts from a fully masked sequence and iteratively unmasks it using a low confidence remasking schedule. Against LLaMA3 8B, LLaDA base scored 65.9 versus 65.4 on MMLU, 35.4 versus 34.8 on HumanEval, and notably 70.3 versus 48.7 on GSM8K, and it surpassed LLaMA2 7B across 15 benchmarks overall. On a poem completion test for the reversal curse it scored 45.6 percent on reversed generation versus GPT-4o's 34.3 percent, beating GPT-4o on that specific task despite trailing it on forward generation. The authors themselves list concrete limitations, no KV caching or the specialized attention optimizations autoregressive models use for fast inference, no reinforcement learning alignment applied, generation length fixed as a hyperparameter rather than adaptive, and direct scaling comparisons validated only up to roughly 10 to the 23rd FLOPs.

papers.note: The standard multimodal survey, covering architecture, training strategy, hallucination and evaluation.
papers.title: A survey on multimodal large language models
papers.explain_beginner: As language models learned to read and write text extremely well, researchers began asking whether the same core model could also be taught to see, meaning take in an image alongside text and reason about both together, without training an entirely separate system from scratch. Yin and coauthors surveyed this fast growing area, called multimodal large language models, cataloging how systems like GPT-4V and open alternatives such as LLaVA and BLIP-2 are typically built and trained. They describe a common recipe, a pretrained image or audio encoder is connected to a pretrained language model through a lightweight connector, then the combined system is trained in stages, first to align the image and text representations, then to follow instructions, then to match human preferences. The survey found that despite fast progress, these systems still confidently describe things that are not actually in the image, a problem called multimodal hallucination, and that most systems remain heavily English centric and limited to whole image understanding rather than fine grained regions or pixels, gaps the field has not yet closed.
papers.explain_business: The strategic read for a business evaluating multimodal AI, models that can process images and documents together with text, is that the underlying architecture pattern, encoder plus connector plus language model, trained in alignment then instruction then preference stages, has converged across both proprietary systems like GPT-4V and open alternatives, which means switching cost between multimodal vendors is likely to keep falling as the open ecosystem catches up. The unresolved gaps the survey documents are directly relevant to deployment risk, multimodal hallucination means a system can misdescribe an uploaded image or document with full confidence, which matters for any workflow, like compliance review or medical imaging triage, where an incorrect visual claim has real consequences, and the English centric training data means non-English visual and text tasks are likely to underperform benchmarks reported in English. Neither gap is close to resolved as of this survey, so human review remains necessary for any high stakes multimodal deployment today.
papers.explain_practitioner: This survey formalizes multimodal large language models as three connected components, a frozen or lightly tuned modality encoder for images, audio, or video, a large language model that does the actual reasoning, and a modality interface connecting them, using either token level fusion, where visual features become extra input tokens, or feature level fusion, where cross attention modules are inserted inside the language model. Training follows three stages the authors document across dozens of surveyed systems, pretraining for cross modal alignment on caption style data, instruction tuning on formatted task data, and alignment tuning using RLHF or DPO to match human preferences, echoing the pipeline used for text only models but applied across modalities. Rather than one benchmark score, the paper's evidence is its systematic coverage of the field's emergent behaviors, in context learning and chain of thought reasoning extended into the visual domain, and its documentation of unresolved technical gaps, multimodal hallucination, limited support for fine grained spatial or pixel level grounding, and a training and evaluation ecosystem still concentrated in English.

papers.note: First sparse model to reach state of the art on transfer learning, and a practical design guide for instability.
papers.title: ST-MoE: Designing Stable and Transferable Sparse Expert Models
papers.explain_beginner: Sparse expert models, which activate only a fraction of their total parameters for each input, promise to grow AI models to huge sizes without paying for all of that size in computation, but in practice earlier versions of these models were often unstable during training and performed inconsistently once fine tuned on a new, specific task. Zoph and coauthors set out to find and fix the specific causes of that instability and unreliable fine tuning, rather than proposing a totally new architecture. Their resulting model, ST-MoE, scaled up to 269 billion total parameters while costing roughly the same computation to run as a dense, non-sparse model with only 32 billion parameters, and it became the first sparse model of this kind to reach state of the art results on a broad transfer learning benchmark suite spanning reasoning, question answering, and summarization tasks. What the paper does not fully resolve is fine tuning on small datasets, the authors' own results show the sparse model still underperforms a comparable dense model on at least one small benchmark with only a few hundred training examples, showing the instability problem is reduced but not eliminated.
papers.explain_business: The business case here is straightforward on compute, a 269 billion parameter model that runs at the cost of a 32 billion parameter dense model is a meaningful infrastructure saving for anyone serving a model at that scale, and the state of the art results across question answering and summarization tasks suggest real output quality gains rather than just parameter count for its own sake. The limitation a buyer or builder needs to weigh is that this efficiency does not extend evenly to every downstream task, the authors' own numbers show the sparse model still loses to smaller dense baselines on tasks with very little fine tuning data, and needs more memory to store parameters even when compute is cheaper. In practice this means sparse expert architectures fit organizations serving broad, high volume tasks with reasonably large task specific datasets, and are a weaker choice for niche applications that only have a small amount of labeled data to fine tune on, where a smaller dense model may still generalize better.
papers.explain_practitioner: ST-MoE contributes a router z-loss and other targeted regularization and initialization changes that stabilize Mixture-of-Experts training, combined with fine tuning guidance addressing the quality and quantity tradeoff, sparse models are more prone to overfit small fine tuning datasets than their dense counterparts. Scaled to ST-MoE-32B, 269 billion total parameters with the training and inference FLOPs of a roughly 32 billion parameter dense transformer, the model reached state of the art transfer learning results across SuperGLUE, ARC Easy and Challenge, XSum, CNN-DM, WebQA, Natural Questions, Winogrande, and ANLI R3, the first sparse model reported to do so across this range of tasks. The authors are explicit about the limits, on CB, a SuperGLUE task with only 250 training examples, the sparse model lags its dense counterpart on held out data, on the smaller SQuAD setup ST-MoE-32B's exact match score of 90.8 falls short of the older dense T5-XXL's 91.3, and on closed book TriviaQA it improves over a fine-tuned dense baseline but still falls short of GPT-3 and GLaM. The paper frames these as evidence that sparse models need careful, task aware fine tuning rather than a solved problem.

papers.note: Soft MoE removes token dropping and training instability, the two failure modes that made sparse models hard to operate.
papers.title: From Sparse to Soft Mixtures of Experts
papers.explain_beginner: Mixture of experts models try to get the benefits of a much bigger AI model without paying the full computational cost, by routing each piece of input to only a handful of specialized sub-networks called experts, rather than running the whole model on every input. The catch researchers kept running into is that the routing decision is a hard, all or nothing choice, so some experts get overloaded while others sit idle, training becomes unstable, and information can get dropped entirely when an expert reaches capacity. Puigcerver and coauthors asked whether a softer version of routing, where every expert sees a blended combination of the input rather than a hard assignment, could keep the speed benefits while avoiding those failure modes. They found their approach, Soft MoE, let them scale a vision model to over 40 times the parameters of a standard model while adding only about 2 percent more time to run it, and it beat both regular dense models and prior hard routing mixture of experts models on image recognition accuracy. What is not yet resolved is how well this soft blending idea works for text generation models that must produce one word at a time without looking ahead, since the method was developed and tested on vision tasks.
papers.explain_business: The practical upside for teams running vision models, or other non-autoregressive workloads, is that this method offers a route to much larger effective model capacity, over 40x more parameters in the tested configuration, for barely any extra serving cost, about 2 percent slower, while also removing the training instability that previously made sparse mixture of experts risky to run in production. That is a meaningfully better cost to capability tradeoff than either scaling a dense model or using earlier hard routed sparse models. The condition that matters before adopting it, though, is architecture fit, the technique as published applies to encoder style vision models rather than to the causal, one token at a time decoding used in most deployed chatbots and text generators, so a business built around large language model text generation cannot yet assume this exact recipe applies without adaptation work. Teams evaluating vendors who cite Soft MoE style efficiency gains should ask specifically whether the claim is for an encoder or a causal decoder setting.
papers.explain_practitioner: Soft MoE replaces discrete, hard token to expert routing with a fully differentiable soft assignment, every expert processes a weighted combination of all input tokens rather than a hard selected subset, which removes the token dropping and expert load imbalance that destabilize training in sparse Mixture-of-Experts models like Switch Transformer. The authors evaluate on vision transformer benchmarks, where a Soft MoE Huge/14 configuration with 128 experts across 16 MoE layers reaches over 40 times the parameter count of a dense ViT-Huge/14 while adding only about 2 percent inference time overhead, and it outperforms both the dense ViT baseline and prior sparse routing variants, Tokens Choice and Experts Choice routing, on accuracy at matched or lower compute. Because the mechanism blends information across the entire token sequence to form each expert's input, it fits encoder style, non-causal architectures well, but the authors are explicit that this design does not transfer cleanly to autoregressive decoding, where a model must not let later tokens leak information into earlier ones, which limits its direct use in standard causal language model decoders without further adaptation.

papers.note: Defines small language models by task fit and resource constraint, the reference for on premises and edge deployment questions.
papers.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Small Language Models in the Era of Large Language Models
papers.journal: ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology
papers.explain_beginner: Most people picture AI chatbots as huge programs that only run on giant data center computers. This paper looks at a different and increasingly important category, small language models, versions built to run on a phone, a laptop, or a small business's own server instead of a distant cloud. The researchers survey how these smaller models are built, trained, and used, and how they compare to their much larger cousins. The finding is that smaller models can be surprisingly capable when they are focused on a specific job, matching or beating far larger models on tasks like answering finance or medical questions, and they run fast enough for real time use on ordinary devices. But they still struggle with harder, open ended reasoning, and they need careful training methods, borrowing knowledge from bigger models or trimming down existing ones, to reach that level. The paper argues small models are a genuine second track in AI, not just a lesser version of large ones, especially where privacy, cost, or speed matter more than raw power.
papers.explain_business: For organizations deciding between a large cloud hosted model and something smaller, this survey's message is that the choice is no longer just capability versus cost. In domains with a narrow, well defined task, answering questions in a specific field, classifying text, powering an on device assistant, a small model can match a much larger and more expensive one while running locally, which cuts inference cost, avoids sending sensitive data to a third party API, and responds fast enough for real time use. The tradeoff shows up on harder, open ended reasoning and coding tasks, where bigger cloud models still have a clear edge, and small models typically need extra work, fine-tuning, distillation from a larger teacher model, or compression, to reach strong performance in a given domain. The paper is also candid that testing for reliability and safety in small models lags behind the large model ecosystem, so buyers deploying a small model in a sensitive area should not assume it has been vetted as thoroughly as a major commercial LLM.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors define small language models by two boundaries, large enough to show the specialized abilities a task needs, small enough to run under real resource limits such as mobile memory budgets, and survey the field across five areas, definitions, how SLMs are built, how they are applied, how they are improved, and how trustworthy they are. Coverage includes architecture choices like grouped query attention and state space models, and methods for shrinking large models into small ones, pruning, knowledge distillation, and quantization down to one or two bits. On benchmarks, they report Phi 3 Mini at 2.7 billion parameters matching GPT 4 on a finance question answering set, and a 1.5 billion parameter biomedical model beating a 62 billion parameter general model on medical question answering, while coding and complex reasoning tasks still favor much larger models. The authors are direct about the gap, small models still struggle with multi-step reasoning and nuanced tasks, and note that trustworthiness evaluation for these models remains underdeveloped compared to large language models.

papers.note: Covers the whole lifecycle of running models on constrained hardware, from model design through runtime optimisation. Relevant to our on-device and edge model sections.
papers.title: A Review on Edge Large Language Models: Design, Execution, and Applications
papers.explain_beginner: Large AI language models normally need powerful servers with lots of memory to run, which is why most chatbot apps send your question over the internet to a data center instead of processing it on your phone. This paper reviews the growing body of research on shrinking these models so they can run directly on a phone, watch, or other small device instead. It surveys the main techniques researchers use, compressing a model's internal numbers into simpler formats, trimming out less important parts of the model, and training smaller models to imitate larger ones, along with the specialized phone chips built to run them efficiently. Running AI on device instead of in the cloud means it can work without an internet connection, respond faster since there is no network delay, and keep personal data on the device rather than sending it to a company's servers. The review is a map of current techniques and open problems, not a claim that on device AI already matches full sized cloud models.
papers.explain_business: Companies considering on device AI features, for privacy, offline functionality, or reduced server costs, can use this review as a technical map of which compression techniques and hardware platforms are mature enough to build on today versus which remain research problems. The identified gap between how much compute modern LLMs need and what current mobile and edge chips can provide means realistic on device products right now generally require smaller, purpose built models rather than shrunk versions of frontier scale systems, a distinction that affects both user experience expectations and engineering timelines. The review's point that compact model development is still concentrated among large, well resourced companies is a relevant competitive fact for smaller teams planning to build on open compact models like Phi or Gemma rather than training their own from scratch. This is an active engineering area now, suitable for near term feature planning, not a distant research horizon.
papers.explain_practitioner: This review surveys the full edge LLM deployment pipeline in three stages, model level compression, pre deployment optimization, and runtime inference. It covers quantization approaches from weight only methods like GPTQ and AWQ to combined weight activation methods like SmoothQuant, structured and unstructured pruning techniques such as SparseGPT and LLM-Pruner, and both white box and black box knowledge distillation, alongside compact architectures such as Phi, Gemma, and OpenELM built with efficiency features like grouped query attention. It maps these techniques onto real edge hardware, including Qualcomm Snapdragon and MediaTek Dimensity mobile chips and dedicated NPUs, and onto inference frameworks such as llama.cpp and MLC-LLM. The authors identify a widening gap between the computational demand of LLMs, measured in TFLOPs, and the capacity of edge hardware, measured in TOPS, as the central unresolved constraint, and separately note that catastrophic forgetting during on device continual learning and fragmentation across heterogeneous device hardware remain open engineering problems without standardized solutions.

papers.note: Reaches Mamba quality in 2.35x fewer training steps, evidence that non transformer scaling is economically real.
papers.title: MoE-Mamba: Efficient Selective State Space Models with Mixture of Experts
papers.explain_beginner: Most of today's AI chatbots run on an architecture called the Transformer, but researchers keep looking for faster alternatives. One promising alternative is called Mamba, a type of model that processes text differently and tends to generate answers more quickly. Separately, a technique called Mixture of Experts speeds up big models by only turning on a small, relevant part of the model's internal network for each word, instead of running the whole thing every time. This paper asks what happens when you combine Mamba with Mixture of Experts. The answer is a new model called MoE-Mamba, which reached the same language-modeling quality as a plain Mamba model while needing about two and a third times fewer training steps, and it also beat a comparable Transformer built with Mixture of Experts. It kept Mamba's fast response speed too, suggesting the combination could make future AI models cheaper to train and quicker to run.
papers.explain_business: MoE-Mamba is a research architecture, not a shipped product, so there is nothing to buy or deploy yet based on this paper alone. What matters for anyone tracking AI infrastructure costs is the direction it points, combining an efficient sequence-processing design with selective expert routing cut the number of training steps needed to reach a given quality level by more than half in the tests reported here, and preserved fast inference speed. If similar gains hold up at larger, production-relevant scales, which the authors themselves have not yet tested, foundation model providers could eventually offer models that are cheaper to train and cheaper to run per query than comparable Transformer-based models of similar quality. For now, procurement and technical teams evaluating language model vendors do not need to act on this paper directly, but it is a useful signal to watch when a vendor advertises a state space or mixture of experts based model, since these approaches are the ones this research suggests could reduce compute costs over the next generation of models.
papers.explain_practitioner: MoE-Mamba interleaves Mamba state space model blocks with Switch-style Mixture of Experts layers that route each token to a single expert using softmax-based scoring and a load-balancing loss. The authors trained models with 25 million and 100 million active parameters on the C4 text dataset with a 1024-token context length, comparing against plain Mamba and a Transformer-based Mixture of Experts baseline. At the 100 million parameter scale, MoE-Mamba reached a final log-perplexity of 2.81, better than vanilla Mamba's 2.99 and better than the Transformer-MoE baseline's 2.88, while needing 2.35 times fewer training steps than plain Mamba to match its performance, with a smaller but still real 1.76 times speedup at the 25 million scale. The authors are explicit about scope, their largest tested configuration reached 2.4 billion total parameters, so it remains untested whether the training-efficiency gains persist at the trillion-parameter scale used by today's largest production models, and alternate ways of placing the expert layers inside each Mamba block produced only marginal further gains.

papers.note: Traces architectural evolution through to multimodal models and compares them on technical features rather than marketing claims.
papers.title: Survey of Different Large Language Model Architectures: Trends, Benchmarks, and Challenges
papers.explain_beginner: This survey traces how large language models, the AI systems behind tools like ChatGPT, have evolved architecturally and compares the main families side by side rather than repeating marketing claims. It groups models into three broad design types, ones built to understand text deeply like BERT, ones built to generate text by predicting the next word like the GPT and LLaMA families, and ones built to transform one text into another like translation style models such as T5. It also covers the newer category of multimodal models that handle images and audio alongside text. Rather than just listing model names, the authors evaluate them against a shared set of standard tests covering reading comprehension, common sense, and science questions, so readers can compare capability rather than hype. The paper's value is organizational, helping someone new to the field understand what family a given model belongs to and what that implies, though it does not itself introduce a new model or method.
papers.explain_business: For a team choosing between model families for a new product, this survey's three way architecture split, understanding focused, generation focused, and transformation focused, plus the newer multimodal category, is a practical filter for narrowing vendor and open source options to the right shape of tool before evaluating specific products. Because the comparisons are grounded in named public benchmarks like MMLU and SuperGLUE rather than vendor claims, procurement teams can request the same benchmark scores from vendors to make an apples to apples comparison instead of relying on marketing language. The authors' identification of data scarcity, context window limits, and multimodal alignment as still open technical problems is useful for setting realistic expectations with stakeholders, since promises of unlimited context or seamless image plus text reasoning from any vendor should be verified against these known limitations rather than accepted at face value.
papers.explain_practitioner: This survey categorizes LLM architectures into three families, auto encoding models such as BERT, RoBERTa, and DeBERTa built for contextual understanding, auto regressive models such as the GPT series, LLaMA, and PaLM built for left to right generation, and sequence to sequence models such as T5 and BART built around encoder decoder designs for conditional generation, then extends the comparison to multimodal systems like KOSMOS-1. Model comparisons are grounded in standard benchmarks including MMLU's 57 subject areas, SuperGLUE, HellaSwag, ARC, and WinoGrande for language understanding and reasoning, plus VQA and NLVR2 for cross modal tasks. The authors identify concrete unresolved challenges rather than only celebrating progress, specifically that high quality training data is becoming scarce as models scale, that context window limits and catastrophic forgetting during continual learning remain unsolved, and that cross modal alignment between text and images is still technically difficult to achieve reliably, all flagged as open problems rather than solved by any surveyed architecture.

papers.note: Product key retrieval over a million tiny experts, pushing the granularity limit of sparse scaling.
papers.title: Mixture of A Million Experts
papers.explain_beginner: Big AI language models get better as they get bigger, but making them bigger usually means every part of the model runs on every word it processes, which costs more computing time and electricity. One fix is to split a model into many small specialist sub-networks, called experts, and only turn on a few for each word. That way a model can hold huge amounts of knowledge without paying the full computing cost every time. The catch is that older systems could only manage a few hundred experts before the bookkeeping of choosing which ones to use became too slow. This paper asks whether a model can use over a million tiny experts instead of a few hundred larger ones, and whether that actually helps. The researchers built a system that searches through a million-plus experts almost instantly, using a trick borrowed from fast database lookups. In their tests, models built this way produced more accurate text predictions than both ordinary models and older expert-based models using the same amount of computing power.
papers.explain_business: This is a research-stage architecture change, not a deployable product feature yet. It matters commercially because it targets the core cost driver of large language models: the tradeoff between how much a model knows and how much compute it burns per query. If the million-expert approach holds up at production scale, it points toward future models that pack in more capability without a proportional rise in serving cost per token, which would eventually show up as cheaper or more capable AI offerings. For now, buyers and deployers of AI should treat this as a signal of where model architectures may be heading rather than something to evaluate in a vendor's current lineup. There is no evidence yet on latency, memory footprint in live serving, or behavior outside language modeling, so anyone comparing vendor claims about more efficient models should ask whether those claims rest on compute-matched evidence like this, or on marketing language borrowing similar vocabulary without it.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper introduces PEER, a layer that replaces a transformer's feedforward block with retrieval over more than one million tiny single-neuron experts. It uses a product key technique, splitting each query into two halves compared against separate key sets, so top matches are found in roughly square-root time instead of scanning every expert. Models were pretrained on C4 at two fixed compute budgets and evaluated by perplexity on Curation Corpus, LAMBADA, the Pile, Wikitext, and C4 validation. At matched compute, PEER beat dense feedforward layers, a coarse 128-expert mixture-of-experts baseline, and product-key memory baselines across all five benchmarks, with expert utilization staying near 100 percent once a batch-normalization fix reduced how unevenly experts were used. The authors note real limits: the work swaps only one feedforward layer per block, tests language modeling exclusively, and reports no inference latency or throughput at scale, leaving efficient serving of million-expert layers, and the specialized hardware kernels it would need, an open question.

papers.note: Combines state space models with mixture of experts and open sources the weights, a live alternative to transformer scaling.
papers.title: BlackMamba: Mixture of Experts for State-Space Models
papers.explain_beginner: The question is whether a language model can be made faster and cheaper to run without losing much of the intelligence people expect from today's largest AI systems. The paper introduces BlackMamba, which combines two ideas, a memory-efficient architecture called a state space model that avoids the slowdown ordinary AI models experience with long text, and a mixture of experts technique that activates only part of the model for each word instead of the whole network. The authors trained two versions, with roughly 1.5 billion and 2.8 billion total parameters, on 300 billion words worth of text, and released the resulting models and code publicly for anyone to use. They found their combined design ran noticeably faster than both plain state space models and standard transformer-based models of similar size, especially when generating long pieces of text, while scoring competitively with those alternatives on common language understanding tests.
papers.explain_business: For a company evaluating which model architecture to build products on, BlackMamba is a research signal rather than a production-ready system. Because both weights and code were released openly, teams can experiment with it directly instead of waiting for a vendor offering, and its constant-latency generation could matter for products handling long documents or long conversations where standard transformer costs climb with every additional word. That said, the released models are small by current standards and were evaluated only on generic multiple-choice style benchmarks, with no testing for safety issues such as toxicity or factual reliability, so nothing here supports deploying it as-is in a customer-facing product without further evaluation. The realistic near-term impact is on infrastructure and research direction rather than immediate purchasing decisions, this work shows mixture of experts and state space designs can be combined successfully, a combination that vendors chasing lower inference cost are likely to build further on.
papers.explain_practitioner: The method is a hybrid architecture combining a Mamba state space model with mixture of experts routing, trained from scratch rather than adapted from an existing model. Training used 300 billion tokens sampled from a larger 1.8 trillion token pool built from The Pile, SlimPajama, Starcoder, PeS2o and ProofPile, covering less than one full pass over that pool. Two model sizes were released, roughly 340 million and 630 million active parameters with 1.5 billion and 2.8 billion total parameters respectively. On zero-shot benchmarks including HellaSwag, PIQA, WinoGrande and Lambada, the models performed competitively with same-size Mamba and transformer baselines, for example the smaller model's average downstream score beat its closest Mamba comparison. The result that matters is architectural, constant-latency generation regardless of sequence length with no key-value cache requirement, alongside lower training and inference compute than dense transformers of comparable quality. The limitation the authors state is that only zero-shot evaluation was run, no safety-related testing for toxicity or factual accuracy was performed, and with just two model sizes trained they say firm scaling conclusions cannot be drawn.

papers.note: A production grade system combining linear sequence modeling with sparse activation, relevant to inference cost planning.
papers.title: Linear-MoE: Linear Sequence Modeling Meets Mixture-of-Experts
papers.explain_beginner: Large language models are often slow and memory-hungry because their attention mechanism gets more expensive as sentences or documents get longer. Meanwhile, another technique called mixture-of-experts lets a model use only a small part of its overall capacity for each word, saving computation. This paper asks whether these two efficiency ideas, a leaner way of processing sequences and mixture-of-experts, can be combined into one system without hurting how well the model performs. The researchers built a framework called Linear-MoE that puts both ideas together, and tested it on models ranging from a few hundred million to seven billion parameters. They found that pure Linear-MoE models kept memory use and speed steady even as text got much longer, unlike standard models which slowed down and used more memory as length grew. Mixing some regular attention layers back in, forming a hybrid design, produced the best overall results on common benchmark tests. The tradeoff is that fully linear models struggled somewhat with tasks needing precise recall of earlier details in a conversation.
papers.explain_business: For teams building or buying large language models, Linear-MoE points to a practical way to cut inference and training costs for long-document or long-conversation use cases, since memory and throughput stay flat as context length grows instead of degrading the way standard transformer attention does. That matters for products handling long chat histories, large codebases, or lengthy documents, where cost and latency currently scale poorly. The results suggest hybrid architectures, mixing a minority of standard attention layers with mostly linear layers, currently offer the best balance of speed and accuracy, so organizations evaluating vendors or open models should ask whether a hybrid design is used rather than a pure linear one. This is still a research-stage architecture tested at modest scale, up to seven billion parameters, not yet proven at the scale of today's largest commercial models, so procurement decisions should treat efficiency claims as promising but not yet validated for production-scale deployments. Recall-heavy tasks, like precisely retrieving a fact from far back in a conversation, remain a weaker point worth testing before adoption.
papers.explain_practitioner: Linear-MoE unifies three families of linear-complexity sequence models, linear attention, state space models, and linear RNNs, with mixture-of-experts layers, and adds a sequence-parallelism training scheme so long contexts train efficiently, including in hybrid stacks that alternate linear and standard transformer blocks. Models were pretrained on a SlimPajama subset, with the smaller A0.3B-2B series trained on 15 billion tokens and the larger A1B-7B series on 100 billion tokens, then evaluated on PiQA, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, and 5-shot MMLU. At 16K token sequence lengths, Linear-MoE variants held throughput near 110-120K tokens per second and memory near 42-43GB, while standard attention throughput fell from about 102K to 49K tokens per second over the same range. On benchmarks, hybrid Linear-MoE with Mamba2 reached 42.70% average accuracy versus 35.53% for the standard attention baseline. Engineering optimizations like grouped GEMM and expert parallelism cut per-step time and per-GPU memory substantially. The authors note pure Linear-MoE models still underperform on recall-heavy tasks such as in-context learning and long-context reasoning, and that scaling behavior beyond the tested model sizes remains untested.

papers.note: Matches a dense Mamba needing 2.3x more active parameters, a concrete efficiency number for the state space line.
papers.title: Routing Mamba: Scaling State Space Models with Mixture-of-Experts Projection
papers.explain_beginner: State space models like Mamba are a newer, more efficient alternative to the standard attention-based design used in most AI language models, but making them bigger and more capable without a huge added cost is tricky. Simply adding mixture-of-experts, a popular trick for scaling up other AI models cheaply, does not work well when bolted onto Mamba in the obvious way, it can actually make performance worse. This paper introduces a new method called Routing Mamba that fixes this by having a single shared decision-maker choose which specialized expert components to use across several parts of the model at once, rather than each part deciding independently. Tested at a scale of about 1.3 billion actively used parameters, this approach matched the performance of a standard Mamba model more than twice its effective size, while saving on the computation needed, cutting required calculations by roughly a quarter in one hybrid setup. The tradeoff is that the researchers are not yet sure how well the exact design will carry over to every future variant of these models.
papers.explain_business: Routing Mamba is a research result rather than a shipped product, but it signals a path toward materially cheaper long-sequence language models, matching a dense model's quality with less than half its effective active-parameter cost, and cutting training compute by about 23 percent in one hybrid configuration tested. For organizations evaluating alternatives to standard transformer-based models, especially for use cases involving very long inputs where Mamba-style architectures already have an efficiency edge, this suggests mixture-of-experts scaling can be added to state space models without the performance penalty earlier naive attempts produced, so it is worth watching whether commercial model providers adopt this kind of shared-routing design. Nothing here changes near-term buying decisions directly, since the method was tested only up to 1.3 billion active parameters and has not been validated at the scale of today's leading commercial models, nor across the full range of competing architectures. The practical takeaway for now is to treat efficient mixture-of-experts variants of state space models as a promising but still maturing option, worth revisiting as larger-scale results appear.
papers.explain_practitioner: Routing Mamba (RoM) addresses a documented failure mode, naive mixture-of-experts integration into Mamba's projection layers degrades rather than improves performance. The method's key idea is a shared router, one routing decision applied jointly across the Conv, Gate, and Output projection layers of a Mamba block, rather than separate independent routers per layer, which the authors argue avoids conflicting expert selections and encourages coordinated specialization. Models were pretrained on 20 billion tokens of SlimPajama at sequence lengths of 4K, 8K, and 16K, and evaluated by perplexity plus downstream accuracy on LAMBADA, HellaSwag, PIQA, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, and WinoGrande, across scales from 115 million to 1.3 billion active parameters. The headline result is that a 1.3B-active, 10B-total RoM model matches the perplexity of a dense Mamba model needing over 2.3 times more active parameters, and RoM combined with FFN-based mixture-of-experts on a Mamba-attention hybrid architecture yields a 23 percent reduction in training compute for equivalent performance. The authors' stated limitation is uncertainty about RoM's optimal configuration and how well it generalizes to the fast-evolving landscape of other state space, attention, and linear-attention variants.
